title: Word formation: diminutives, feminine forms and possessive adjectives
objectives: I can recognize a diminutive, say what it adds (smallness, affection, politeness or irony), and form diminutives of nouns and adjectives with '-ик', '-чик', '-к-', '-очк-', '-ечк-', '-оньк-' and '-еньк-'.
I can explain the changes inside 'рука́', 'ру́чка', 'руче́нька', 'нога́', 'ні́жка' and 'кіт', 'ко́тик' with the rules of the earlier units.
I can name a woman by her profession with '-ка', '-иця' or '-иня', as standard Ukrainian does today.
I can say whose something is with possessive adjectives such as 'ма́мин', 'та́тів', 'Оле́нин' and 'Андрі́їв', and make them agree with the thing owned in every case.
I can split a word into prefix, root, suffix and ending, and connect the words of one family, such as 'писа́ти', 'напи́с', 'письмо́' and 'письме́нник'.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'мали́й' with the suffix '-еньк-'. It is the everyday word for 'little' and sounds warmer than 'мали́й', which states size alone. Forms: 'мале́нька', 'мале́ньке', 'мале́нькі'.
Built from 'га́рний' with '-еньк-', and the stress moves onto the suffix. It describes children, small animals and small pretty things, and it can also be said with irony.

Built from 'со́нце' with '-ечк-': the 'ц' becomes 'ч'. It names the sun when people speak of it fondly, and it is one of the most common affectionate words for a child or a loved one. It is also the Ukrainian name of the ladybug.
Built from 'ха́та' with the suffixes '-ин-' and '-к-', and the stress moves to 'ти'. Locative 'у хати́нці': 'к' becomes 'ц' before '-і', as in 'у руці́'.

example.target: Бабу́ся живе́ в мале́нькій хати́нці бі́ля лі́су.
example.source: Grandma lives in a little cottage near the forest.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'рука́' with '-еньк-', and 'к' becomes 'ч' before the suffix. 'Ру́чка', the plainer diminutive, has become the everyday word for a pen and a handle, so 'руче́нька' is the form that clearly means a small hand and sounds the most tender.
Built from 'нога́' with '-к-': 'г' becomes 'ж', and 'о' becomes 'і' because the first syllable is now closed. It also names the leg of a table or a chair.

example.source: The table stands on four legs.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ко́тика'. Built from 'кіт' with '-ик'. The suffix opens the syllable, so 'і' returns to 'о', as in 'кота́'. It names a young cat or any cat spoken of fondly, and it is a pet name for a loved one: 'Ко́тику!'

example.target: Наш ко́тик лю́бить спа́ти на вікні́.
example.source: Our kitty loves to sleep on the windowsill.
example.source_literal: Our kitty loves to-sleep on window.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'хло́пець': the suffix '-ець' gives way to '-чик'. It is the usual word for a boy up to about twelve, and 'хло́пець' is for an older boy or a young man. Genitive 'хло́пчика'.

example.target: Хло́пчик гра́є у футбо́л у па́рку.
example.source: A little boy is playing soccer in the park.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'ді́вчина' with '-к-', and the stress moves to 'чи'. It is the usual word for a girl up to about twelve. Dative and locative 'дівчи́нці'.

example.source: This little girl draws very well.

vocabulary.note: Made from 'ма́ма' with '-ин'. It agrees with the thing owned, like 'мій': 'ма́мина', 'ма́мине', 'ма́мині'.
Made from 'та́то' with '-ів'. In every other form an ending opens the syllable and 'і' becomes 'о': 'та́това', 'та́тове', 'та́тові'.

example.source: Dad's shoes are by the door.

vocabulary.note: The author of any text: a book, an article, a song. Genitive 'а́втора'. A woman is 'а́вторка'. In the example, 'ціє́ї' is the genitive of 'ця', formed like 'моє́ї'.
Made from 'а́втор' with '-ка', and like most nouns in '-ка' it keeps the stress of the masculine noun. It is the usual word today in books, the press and public life.

example.source: She is the author of this book.

vocabulary.note: The person who leads a team, a department or an organization. Genitive 'керівника́': the stress moves to the ending. The 'в' ends a syllable and is said [w].

example.source: Our manager is on vacation today.

vocabulary.note: Made from 'керівни́к' with '-иця', which takes the place of '-ик'. The plural 'керівни́ці' names women only.

example.source: She is the head of a large hospital.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'письме́нника'. A writer of literature: novels, stories, poems. The word for the person who wrote a particular article is 'а́втор'. A woman is 'письме́нниця'. The doubled 'нн' is one long [nː].

example.target: Цей письме́нник пи́ше кни́ги для діте́й.
example.source: This writer writes books for children.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'друг' with the suffix '-б-': 'г' becomes 'ж' before it, as in the vocative 'дру́же'.
Built on the root of 'писа́ти'. It names a writing system and the act of writing: 'украї́нське письмо́', the Ukrainian script. The everyday word for a letter you send is 'лист'.

example.target: Украї́нське письмо́ ма́є три́дцять три лі́тери.
example.source: The Ukrainian script has thirty-three letters.
example.source_literal: Ukrainian script has thirty three letters.

vocabulary.note: The prefix 'на-', on, and the root of 'писа́ти': something written on a surface, such as a sign, a label or the words on a T-shirt. Genitive 'напи́су'.

dialogues.title: In the park with Grandma
dialogues.context: Halyna, Oksana's mother, is in the park with her granddaughter Mariika, who is four. Sam has come with Oksana, who has gone to buy coffee. Halyna and Mariika say 'ти' to each other; Sam says 'ви' to Halyna and calls her 'па́ні Гали́но', and she says 'ти' to him.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Марі́йко, со́нечко! Іди́ сюди́ й дай бабу́сі руче́ньку.
lines.source: Mariika, sweetheart! Come here and give Grandma your hand.
lines.source_literal: Mariika, little-sun! Go here and give to-grandma little-hand.

lines.speaker: Марі́йка
lines.target: Бабу́сю, там ко́тик! Мале́нький, сі́ренький!
lines.source: Grandma, there's a kitty over there! A little gray one!
lines.source_literal: Grandma, there kitty! Little, gray-little!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Па́ні Гали́но, мо́жна запита́ти? Чому́ ви ка́жете «руче́нька», а не «рука́»?
lines.source: Ms. Halyna, may I ask something? Why do you say 'руче́нька' and not 'рука́'?
lines.source_literal: Ms. Halyna, possible to-ask? Why you say 'little-hand', and not 'hand'?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Бо вона́ ще мале́нька. З дітьми́ ми так гово́римо: не рука́, а руче́нька, не нога́, а ні́жка.
lines.source: Because she's still little. That's how we talk to children: not 'рука́' but 'руче́нька', not 'нога́' but 'ні́жка'.
lines.source_literal: Because she still little. With children we so speak: not hand, but little-hand, not leg, but little-leg.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А «ко́тик»? Це мали́й кіт?
lines.source: And 'ко́тик'? Is that a small cat?
lines.source_literal: And 'kitty'? This small cat?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Не завжди́. Наш кіт уже́ стари́й і вели́кий, але́ ми ка́жемо «ко́тик», бо ми його́ ду́же лю́бимо.
lines.source: Not always. Our cat is old and big now, but we say 'ко́тик' because we love him very much.
lines.source_literal: Not always. Our cat already old and big, but we say 'kitty', because we him very love.

lines.speaker: Марі́йка
lines.target: Бабу́сю, я хо́чу ї́сти! Де моє́ я́блучко?
lines.source: Grandma, I'm hungry! Where's my apple?
lines.source_literal: Grandma, I want to-eat! Where my little-apple?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Ось твоє́ я́блучко й ча́шечка со́ку.
lines.source: Here's your apple and a little cup of juice.
lines.source_literal: Here your little-apple and little-cup of-juice.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А чия́ це ку́ртка? Ва́ша?
lines.source: And whose jacket is this? Yours?
lines.source_literal: And whose this jacket? Yours?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Ні, це Окса́нина ку́ртка. Вона́ пішла́ в Андрі́єве кафе́.
lines.source: No, it's Oksana's jacket. She went to Andrii's café.
lines.source_literal: No, this Oksana's jacket. She went in Andrii's café.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́нина, Андрі́єве... Це як «Окса́ни» й «Андрі́я»?
lines.source: Oksana's, Andrii's... Is that like 'Окса́ни' and 'Андрі́я'?
lines.source_literal: Oksana's, Andrii's... This like of-Oksana and of-Andrii?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Так. Так ми ка́жемо про люде́й, яки́х до́бре зна́ємо.
lines.source: Yes. That's how we talk about people we know well.
lines.source_literal: Yes. So we say about people, whom well we-know.

lines.speaker: Марі́йка
lines.target: Бабу́сю, а я твоя́ дівчи́нка?
lines.source: Grandma, am I your little girl?
lines.source_literal: Grandma, and I your little-girl?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Моя́, со́нечко. Ході́мо додо́му.
lines.source: Yes, you are, sweetheart. Let's go home.
lines.source_literal: Mine, little-sun. Let's-go home.

dialogues.title: A notice at the hospital
dialogues.context: Olena, a doctor, and Bohdan, who works in the hospital office, have worked together for years and say 'ти'. Bohdan has written a notice about the hospital's new head and asks Olena to check it before he puts it up. 'Хіру́рг' means a surgeon.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Оле́но, прочита́й, будь ла́ска, оголо́шення. Тут нема́є поми́лок?
lines.source: Olena, please read the notice. Are there any mistakes?
lines.source_literal: Olena, read, please, notice. Here there-is-not of-mistakes?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: «Нови́й керівни́к на́шої лі́карні: Мари́на Іва́нівна Ковале́нко». Богда́не, а чому́ «керівни́к»?
lines.source: 'New head of our hospital: Maryna Ivanivna Kovalenko.' Bohdan, why 'керівни́к'?
lines.source_literal: 'New head of-our hospital: Maryna Ivanivna Kovalenko.' Bohdan, and why 'head'?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: А як тре́ба? Я ду́мав, що в оголо́шеннях пи́шуть «керівни́к».
lines.source: What should it be? I thought notices said 'керівни́к'.
lines.source_literal: And how needed? I thought, that in notices they-write 'head'.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Рані́ше так писа́ли. Але́ вона́ жі́нка, тому́ «керівни́ця». Тепе́р і в докуме́нтах ча́сто пи́шуть «керівни́ця» чи «дире́кторка».
lines.source: People used to write it that way. But she's a woman, so it's 'керівни́ця'. Now even documents often say 'керівни́ця' or 'дире́кторка'.
lines.source_literal: Earlier so they-wrote. But she woman, therefore 'head-woman'. Now and in documents often they-write 'head-woman' or 'director-woman'.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́бре, перепишу́. А як написа́ти про нову́ лі́карку зі Льво́ва? Вона́ працю́є хіру́ргом.
lines.source: All right, I'll rewrite it. And how should I write about the new doctor from Lviv? She works as a surgeon.
lines.source_literal: Good, I-will-rewrite. And how to-write about new doctor-woman from Lviv? She works by-surgeon.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Хіру́ргиня. Так са́мо, як продавчи́ня.
lines.source: 'Хіру́ргиня', the same way as 'продавчи́ня'.
lines.source_literal: Surgeon-woman. So same, as shop-assistant-woman.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Хіру́ргиня... Я тако́го сло́ва ще не чув.
lines.source: 'Хіру́ргиня'... I've never heard that word before.
lines.source_literal: Surgeon-woman... I of-such word still not heard.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Це нове́ сло́во, але́ че́рез рік ти до ньо́го зви́кнеш.
lines.source: It's a new word, but in a year you'll be used to it.
lines.source_literal: This new word, but in year you to it will-get-used.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Мо́же. А що написа́ти про те́бе? «Лі́кар»?
lines.source: Maybe. And what should I write about you? 'Лі́кар'?
lines.source_literal: Maybe. And what to-write about you? 'Doctor'?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Лі́карка, звича́йно! Я лі́карка вже де́сять ро́ків.
lines.source: 'Лі́карка', of course! I've been a doctor for ten years.
lines.source_literal: Doctor-woman, of course! I doctor-woman already ten years.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую! За́втра ти поба́чиш нове́ оголо́шення.
lines.source: Thanks! Tomorrow you'll see the new notice.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Tomorrow you will-see new notice.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: І не забу́дь: керівни́ця, а не керівни́к!
lines.source: And don't forget: 'керівни́ця', not 'керівни́к'!
lines.source_literal: And not forget: head-woman, and not head!

dialogues.title: One root, many words
dialogues.context: After class Sam stays to ask his teacher, Iryna Petrivna, about words that look alike. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'Схо́жий' means similar, 'дружи́ти' means to be friends, and 'утво́рений від' means formed from.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, «писа́ти», «напи́с» і «письме́нник» ду́же схо́жі. У них оди́н ко́рінь?
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, 'писа́ти', 'напи́с' and 'письме́нник' look very similar. Do they have the same root?
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, 'to-write', 'inscription' and 'writer' very similar. At them one root?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, Се́ме, ко́рінь у них оди́н. Які́ ще слова́ з цим ко́ренем ви зна́єте?
lines.source: Yes, Sam, they share one root. What other words with this root do you know?
lines.source_literal: Yes, Sam, root at them one. Which else words with this root you know?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: «Пі́дпис» і «підписа́ти». А ще «письмо́»?
lines.source: 'Пі́дпис' and 'підписа́ти'. And 'письмо́' too?
lines.source_literal: 'Signature' and 'to-sign'. And also 'writing'?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: І «письмо́» теж. Украї́нське письмо́ ви вже зна́єте: усі́ три́дцять три лі́тери.
lines.source: 'Письмо́' too. You already know the Ukrainian script: all thirty-three letters.
lines.source_literal: And 'writing' too. Ukrainian script you already know: all thirty three letters.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А чому́ в сло́ві «письме́нник» є м’яки́й знак?
lines.source: And why is there a soft sign in the word 'письме́нник'?
lines.source_literal: And why in word 'writer' is soft sign?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Бо це сло́во утво́рене від «письмо́», а там м’яки́й знак уже́ є.
lines.source: Because the word is made from 'письмо́', and that word already has one.
lines.source_literal: Because this word formed from 'writing', and there soft sign already is.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Зрозумі́в. А «дру́жба» від «друг»?
lines.source: I see. And 'дру́жба' comes from 'друг'?
lines.source_literal: Understood. And 'friendship' from 'friend'?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так. І «по́друга», і «дружи́на».
lines.source: Yes. And 'по́друга', and 'дружи́на' too.
lines.source_literal: Yes. And 'friend-woman', and 'wife'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: «Дружи́на»? Це тому́, що чолові́к і дружи́на дру́жать?
lines.source: 'Дружи́на'? Is that because a husband and wife are friends?
lines.source_literal: 'Wife'? This because, that husband and wife are-friends?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Га́рна ду́мка! Але́ ти́сячу ро́ків тому́ це сло́во означа́ло щось і́нше.
lines.source: A nice thought! But a thousand years ago the word meant something else.
lines.source_literal: Nice thought! But thousand years ago this word meant something other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А я вже дружу́ з украї́нським письмо́м!
lines.source: And I'm already friends with the Ukrainian script!
lines.source_literal: And I already am-friends with Ukrainian script!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ба́чу, Се́ме. І ця дру́жба вам допомага́є.
lines.source: I can see that, Sam. And this friendship is helping you.
lines.source_literal: I-see, Sam. And this friendship to-you helps.

grammar.title: Diminutives: small and dear
grammar.explanation:
A diminutive is a noun or an adjective made from another word with a suffix, a part added to a word before its ending to make a new word. It presents the thing as small, as dear to the speaker, or both. 'Кіт' is a cat, and 'ко́тик' is a kitten or a cat spoken of fondly; 'рука́' is a hand, and 'руче́нька' is a little hand. English has a few such endings, as in 'kitty' and 'booklet', but Ukrainian can form a diminutive from almost any noun, and speakers use them every day.

A diminutive keeps the gender of the word it comes from, so it agrees in the same way: 'кіт' and 'ко́тик' are masculine, 'рука́' and 'руче́нька' feminine, 'со́нце' and 'со́нечко' neuter. The suffix stands before the ending, and the ending changes for case as usual: 'з ко́тиком', 'у хати́нці'.

The suffix depends on the gender of the noun:

- Masculine nouns take '-ик' or '-чик': 'кіт', 'ко́тик'; 'ніс', 'но́сик'; 'брат', 'бра́тик'. '-ик' is far more common, and the word decides which one it takes. In 'хло́пчик', from 'хло́пець', '-чик' takes the place of '-ець'.
- Feminine nouns take '-к-' before the ending '-а': 'нога́', 'ні́жка'; 'рука́', 'ру́чка'; 'ді́вчина', 'дівчи́нка'. 'Хати́нка' adds '-ин-' and '-к-' to 'ха́та'.
- Feminine nouns also take '-очк-' after a hard consonant and '-ечк-' after a soft one, and '-ечк-' replaces the '-к-' of a noun that already has it: 'ма́ма', 'ма́мочка'; 'до́нька', 'до́нечка'; 'ло́жка', 'ло́жечка'; 'ча́шка', 'ча́шечка'.
- Feminine nouns take '-оньк-' or '-еньк-' for the most tender forms, heard in songs and in speech to children. '-еньк-' follows a soft consonant or 'ж', 'ч' and 'ш', and '-оньк-' the other hard consonants: 'рука́', 'руче́нька'; 'ри́ба', 'ри́бонька'.
- Neuter nouns take '-к-' before '-о', or '-ечк-': 'я́блуко', 'я́блучко'; 'ву́хо', 'ву́шко'; 'со́нце', 'со́нечко'; 'мі́сто', 'місте́чко'.

Adjectives take '-еньк-' before their usual endings: 'мали́й', 'мале́нький'; 'га́рний', 'гарне́нький'; 'нови́й', 'нове́нький'; 'сі́рий', 'сі́ренький'. They agree like any adjective: 'мале́нька дівчи́нка', 'гарне́нькі ні́жки'. 'Малю́сінький' and 'мале́сенький' go one step further and mean 'tiny'.

A diminutive often has a stress of its own, which you learn with the word: 'рука́', 'ру́чка', 'руче́нька'; 'ха́та', 'хати́нка'; 'ді́вчина', 'дівчи́нка'. The consonant and vowel changes inside these words are explained in the spelling note of this unit.

examples.target: Марі́йка ще мале́нька, їй чоти́ри ро́ки.
examples.source: Mariika is still little; she is four.
examples.source_literal: Mariika still little, to-her four years.

examples.source: The little boy is eating an apple.
Could I have a teaspoon, please?

examples.target: Ми жили́ в мале́нькому місте́чку бі́ля Льво́ва.
examples.source: We lived in a small town near Lviv.
Mommy, I love you!

grammar.title: What a diminutive says: affection, politeness, irony
grammar.explanation:
A diminutive often says less about size than about the speaker's attitude. The same suffix can carry several meanings, and the situation and the tone of voice decide which one is meant.

Affection is the most common. Parents and grandparents speak to children in diminutives, and partners and close friends use them as pet names: 'со́нечко', 'ко́тику', 'ри́бонько'. First names have affectionate forms too: 'Окса́нка' from 'Окса́на', 'Тара́сик' from 'Тара́с', 'Марі́йка' from 'Марі́я', and 'Андрі́йко' from 'Андрі́й', with the masculine '-к-' before the ending '-о'. Such a name is used only by family and close friends, never with 'па́ні' or with a patronymic.

Politeness is the second. A diminutive makes a request or an offer sound smaller and friendlier, so people use them in shops, in cafés and at home with guests:

- 'Хвили́нку!', literally 'little-minute', asks someone to wait.
- 'Вам паке́тик?', literally 'to-you little-bag?', is a shop assistant's offer of a bag.
- 'Ще ча́шечку ка́ви?', literally 'more little-cup of-coffee?', is a host's offer.

This use is not childish, but in formal writing, at a meeting or in a letter the plain words are the right choice.

Irony is the third. Said of something large or unpleasant, a diminutive means the opposite of what it says. 'Гарне́нька хати́нка: три по́верхи й два балко́ни!' mocks a house that is anything but a cottage.

Some diminutives have become words of their own, and the meaning of smallness has faded:

- 'ру́чка' is a pen or a handle
- 'ні́жка' is also the leg of a table or a chair
- 'ло́жечка' is a teaspoon
- 'місте́чко' is a small town
- 'кни́жка' is an everyday word for a book, as common as 'кни́га'
- 'сто́лик' is the usual word for a table in a café

So 'вели́ка кни́жка' is simply a big book, and 'Є ві́льний сто́лик?' asks for any free table.

rows: to a child or a loved one
to a friend or a relative, fondly

grammar.title: A woman's profession: '-ка', '-иця', '-иня'
grammar.explanation:
A noun that names a person by profession, role or origin usually has a masculine form for a man and a feminine form for a woman. Units 8 and 23 taught the pairs 'студе́нт', 'студе́нтка' and 'програмі́ст', 'програмі́стка'. Such a feminine noun is called a feminitive, in Ukrainian 'фемініти́в': 'Такі́ іме́нники назива́ють фемініти́вами.', literally 'such nouns they-call by-feminitives', with 'назива́ти', to call or name, and the instrumental. It is made from the masculine noun with a suffix, and the Ukrainian orthography of 2019, the official rules of spelling, lists '-к-', '-иц-' and '-ин-' among the suffixes for it:

- '-ка' is added to the masculine noun, which keeps its stress in most words: 'лі́кар', 'лі́карка'; 'а́втор', 'а́вторка'; 'дире́ктор', 'дире́кторка'; 'інжене́р', 'інжене́рка'. A soft sign stays: 'вчи́тель', 'вчи́телька'.
- '-иця' takes the place of '-ик' in nouns that end in '-ник' or '-ик': 'керівни́к', 'керівни́ця'; 'письме́нник', 'письме́нниця'; 'співробі́тник', 'співробі́тниця'.
- '-иня' is added to some other nouns, among them those in '-г': 'хіру́рг', surgeon, 'хіру́ргиня'. In 'продаве́ць', 'продавчи́ня' the '-ець' gives way, and 'ч' appears before the suffix.

The nationality words of unit 7 lose '-ець' in the same way before '-ка': 'украї́нець', 'украї́нка'; 'кана́дець', 'кана́дка'.

A feminine noun takes feminine agreement in every word around it: 'на́ша нова́ керівни́ця', 'Керівни́ця прийшла́.' In the plural the masculine form names men or a mixed group, and the feminine form names women only: 'керівники́' against 'керівни́ці'.

The masculine noun also names the profession in general, without thinking of a particular person: 'Тобі́ тре́ба йти до лі́каря.' (You need to see a doctor.) For a particular woman, today's standard Ukrainian uses the feminine noun, in speech, in the press and more and more in documents. Some people, mostly older ones, still use the masculine noun for a woman, especially in official titles. This course always uses the feminine noun for a woman.

A feminine profession also serves in address, with 'па́ні' and the vocative: 'Па́ні лі́карко!', 'Па́ні дире́кторко!'

grammar.title: Possessive adjectives: 'ма́мин', 'та́тів', 'Оле́нин'
grammar.explanation:
Unit 14 taught one way to name an owner: the genitive after the thing owned, 'кни́га Окса́ни', literally 'book of-Oksana'. When the owner is one particular person named by a first name or a family word, Ukrainian has a second way. It turns the owner's noun into an adjective that stands before the thing owned, like 'мій': 'Окса́нина кни́га', Oksana's book. Such a word is a possessive adjective, in Ukrainian 'присві́йний прикме́тник'. It answers the question 'чий?' (whose?), and in everyday speech about family and friends it is more common than the genitive.

Nouns in '-а' or '-я' take '-ин', which replaces the ending:

- 'ма́ма', 'ма́мин'; 'Оле́на', 'Оле́нин'; 'Окса́на', 'Окса́нин'; 'Мико́ла', 'Мико́лин'
- a soft consonant before '-я' becomes hard: 'бабу́ся', 'бабу́син'
- after a vowel or the apostrophe the suffix is '-їн': 'Со́фія', 'Со́фіїн'; 'Марі́я', 'Марі́їн'
- after a doubled soft consonant it is '-ін', as in the man's name 'Ілля́', 'Іллі́н'
- 'к' before the suffix becomes 'ч': 'ті́тка', 'ті́тчин'

Masculine nouns that end in a consonant or in '-о' take '-ів', and after a vowel or 'й', '-їв': 'та́то', 'та́тів'; 'брат', 'бра́тів'; 'Тара́с', 'Тара́сів'; 'діду́сь', 'діду́сів'; 'Андрі́й', 'Андрі́їв'.

A possessive adjective agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner: 'та́тів стіл', 'та́това кни́га', 'та́тове вікно́', 'та́тові череви́ки'. So 'ма́мин телефо́н' is masculine because 'телефо́н' is, although the owner is a woman. A possessive adjective made from a name keeps the capital letter: 'Оле́нин', 'Андрі́їв'.

Only the masculine nominative, and the masculine accusative when the thing owned is not a living being, has the short form 'ма́мин' or 'та́тів'. Every other form takes the endings of a hard adjective such as 'нови́й': 'до Оле́ниного бра́та', 'з ма́миною по́другою', 'у та́товій кімна́ті'. In the forms of '-ів' the endings open the syllable, so 'і' returns to 'о' after a hard consonant and to 'е' after a soft one, written 'є' after a vowel: 'та́това', 'Тара́сова', 'діду́сева', 'Андрі́єва'. The spelling note explains this alternation.

The genitive is still needed in other situations:

- the owner has words of its own: 'кни́га моє́ї ма́ми', 'кни́га Окса́ни Ковале́нко'
- there are several owners: 'кімна́та діте́й'
- the owner is not a person: 'центр мі́ста'

The plural 'та́тові' has the same letters as the dative 'та́тові', to Dad. 'Та́тові череви́ки' are Dad's shoes, while 'Я дав та́тові кни́гу.' means 'I gave Dad a book.' The rest of the sentence decides.

rows: like the nominative or the genitive

grammar.title: Word families: prefix, root, suffix and ending
grammar.explanation:
Most Ukrainian words are built from a few parts, and once you can see them, a new word often explains itself. Ukrainian grammar names four kinds of part:

- the root, 'ко́рінь', the part that carries the basic meaning and that every word of a family shares: 'пис' in 'писа́ти', 'напи́с', 'письмо́'
- a prefix, 'пре́фікс', a part before the root: 'на-' in 'напи́с'
- a suffix, 'су́фікс', a part after the root that makes a new word: '-ар' in 'лі́кар'
- the ending, 'закі́нчення', the last part, which changes for case, number and person: '-о' in 'письмо́', '-и' in 'кни́ги'

A word may have several prefixes or suffixes, or none: 'друг' is a root alone, with no ending in the nominative. Words that share a root form a word family. Ukrainian says that a word is 'утво́рений від', formed from, the word it is built on, with the passive participle of 'утвори́ти', to form, whose imperfective is 'утво́рювати': 'Сло́во «напи́с» утво́рене від «писа́ти».' The family of 'писа́ти' shows how prefixes and suffixes build meaning:

- 'напи́с', 'on' plus 'write': an inscription or a sign
- 'пі́дпис', 'under' plus 'write': a signature, the name written under a text
- 'письмо́', the root with the suffix '-ьм-': writing, a script
- 'письме́нник', built on 'письмо́' with '-енн-' and '-ик': a writer, and 'письме́нниця' for a woman
- 'написа́ти', 'переписа́ти', 'підписа́ти', verbs with prefixes

A root can change a sound inside the family by the alternations you know: 'с' becomes 'ш' in 'пишу́', 'пи́шеш', as 'д' becomes 'дж' in 'ходжу́'. In the family of 'друг', 'г' becomes 'ж' before a suffix and 'з' before the ending '-і': 'дру́жба', friendship; 'дружи́ти', to be friends ('Я дружу́ з Тара́сом.'); 'дру́жній', friendly; 'дру́зі', friends. 'По́друга' adds the prefix 'по-', and 'дружи́на', wife, is an old word of the same family.

Some suffixes have a meaning of their own:

- '-ар', '-тель' and '-ник' name a person who does something: 'лі́кар', 'вчи́тель', 'керівни́к'
- '-н-' before the ending '-я' names a place: 'лі́карня', a hospital, from the root of 'лі́кар', 'лі́ки' and 'лікува́ти', to treat
- '-б-' makes a noun that names a relationship or a quality, not a thing: 'дру́жба'

A compound is a word built from two roots, joined with 'о' or 'е'. 'Роботода́вець', employer, is 'робо́та' plus the root of 'дава́ти', literally 'work-giver', and 'мовозна́вець', linguist, is 'мо́ва' plus the root of 'зна́ти', literally 'language-knower'.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: руче́нька, ні́жка, та́тів and та́това
grammar.explanation:
The new words of this unit show changes that you already know from units 5 and 14. This time a suffix sets them off.

Before the diminutive suffixes '-к-', '-ечк-' and '-еньк-', before the '-ин' of a possessive adjective and before the '-б-' of 'дру́жба', four consonants change:

- 'к' becomes 'ч' [t͡ʃ]: 'рука́', 'ру́чка', 'руче́нька'; 'я́блуко', 'я́блучко'; 'ті́тка', 'ті́тчин'
- 'г' becomes 'ж' [ʒ]: 'нога́', 'ні́жка'; 'кни́га', 'кни́жка'; 'друг', 'дру́жба'
- 'х' becomes 'ш' [ʃ]: 'ву́хо', 'ву́шко'
- 'ц' becomes 'ч' [t͡ʃ]: 'со́нце', 'со́нечко'; 'лиси́ця', fox, 'лиси́чка'

These are the changes of the vocative in unit 14, 'друг', 'дру́же' and 'чолові́к', 'чолові́че'. They differ from the changes before the ending '-і' in unit 5, where 'к' becomes 'ц' and 'г' becomes 'з': 'у руці́', 'у кни́зі'. So one root can show three consonants: 'рука́', 'у руці́', 'руче́нька'.

The vowels follow the rule of unit 5: in a closed syllable, one that ends in a consonant, 'о' and 'е' become 'і'. A suffix can close a syllable or open one:

- 'нога́' is 'но-га́', but in 'ні́жка' the 'ж' closes the first syllable, 'ніж-ка', so 'о' becomes 'і'.
- 'кіт' is one closed syllable, but in 'ко́тик' the suffix opens it, 'ко-тик', so 'і' returns to 'о'; 'ніс' and 'но́сик' are the same.
- 'та́тів' ends in a closed syllable. Every other form adds an ending and opens it, so 'о' returns: 'та́-то-ва'. After a vowel, 'ї' returns to 'є': 'Андрі́їв', 'Андрі́єва', as in 'Ки́їв', 'Ки́єва'.

The patronymic shows the same alternation in an old possessive suffix: 'Петро́вич' is 'Пет-ро́-вич', with 'о' in an open syllable, while 'Петрі́вна' is 'Пет-рі́в-на', with 'і' in a closed one.

Other points in these words:

- 'ж' stays voiced before 'к', as the 'д' of 'сусі́дка' does: 'ні́жка' [ˈnʲiʒkɑ], 'кни́жка' [ˈknɪʒkɑ].
- 'в' at the end of a syllable is [w]: 'та́тів' [ˈtɑtʲiw], 'керівни́к' [kɛrʲiwˈnɪk], 'дівчи́нка' [dʲiwˈt͡ʃɪnkɑ]. Before a vowel it is [ʋ]: 'та́това' [ˈtɑtɔʋɑ].
- The soft sign softens 'н' before 'к' in '-еньк-' and '-оньк-': 'мале́нький' [mɑˈlɛnʲkɪj], 'руче́нька' [ruˈt͡ʃɛnʲkɑ]. It softens 'с' in 'письмо́' [pɪsʲˈmɔ].
- The doubled 'нн' of 'письме́нник' is one long [nː]: [pɪsʲˈmɛnːɪk].
- 'ї' is always [ji], also after 'і': 'Со́фіїн' [ˈsɔfʲijin], 'Андрі́їв' [ɑnˈdrʲijiw].
- In 'керівни́ця' the 'ц' is soft before 'я': [kɛrʲiwˈnɪt͡sʲɑ].
- 'Ко́рінь' has 'і' in its closed last syllable and 'е' where an ending opens it: 'ко́реня', 'ко́ренем'.

before a consonant or at the end of a word

culture.title: Tender words, and cities that belong to someone
culture.text:
Ukrainian is rich in tender words, and the diminutive is their main tool. Lullabies are full of them, and so are folk tales. The word for a lullaby is 'колиско́ва', a feminine noun declined like an adjective: it is the adjective of 'колиска́', a cradle, with 'пі́сня', song, left out. In the best known of the folk tales, 'Рукави́чка' (The Mitten), a grandfather loses a mitten in the winter forest, and one animal after another moves in, each named with a diminutive:

- 'ми́шка', a little mouse
- 'жа́бка', a little frog
- 'за́йчик', a little hare
- 'лиси́чка', a little fox
- 'во́вчик', a little wolf

In the full tale a boar and a bear squeeze in too, and children learn the story by heart.

In everyday life, diminutives are part of how people show warmth:

- the affectionate forms of first names, used in the family and among close friends: 'Окса́нка', 'Тара́сик', 'Марі́йка', 'Андрі́йко'
- pet names for children and partners: 'со́нечко', 'ко́тику', 'ри́бонько'
- small words of hospitality and service: 'Хвили́нку!', 'Ще ча́шечку?', 'Вам паке́тик?'

Some people find too many of them sugary, and in formal settings Ukrainians use the full first name with the patronymic, never a diminutive.

Several Ukrainian cities are named with an old possessive adjective. By legend, Kyiv was founded by three brothers, Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv, and their sister Lybid, and 'Ки́їв' means 'Kyi's town'. Lviv was founded in the thirteenth century by King Danylo and named after his son Lev: 'Львів' is 'Lev's town'. That is why these names change like 'та́тів' and 'Андрі́їв': 'з Ки́єва', 'у Льво́ві'. The patronymic 'Петрі́вна' comes from the same kind of suffix.

The word 'дружи́на' has a history of its own. A thousand years ago, in the state centered on Kyiv, it named the band of companions and warriors who lived and fought with a prince, the people he trusted like friends. Historians still use the word in this sense, while in everyday Ukrainian today it means a wife.

paragraphs.target: Узи́мку діду́сь ішо́в че́рез ліс і загуби́в рукави́чку.
paragraphs.source: One winter Grandpa was walking through the forest and lost his mitten.
paragraphs.source_literal: In-winter grandpa was-going through forest and lost little-mitten.

paragraphs.target: Біжи́ть ми́шка, ба́чить рукави́чку й ка́же: «Тут я бу́ду жи́ти!» І ми́шка почала́ жи́ти в рукави́чці.
paragraphs.source: A little mouse comes running, sees the mitten and says: 'I'll live here!' And so the little mouse began to live in the mitten.
paragraphs.source_literal: Runs little-mouse, sees little-mitten and says: 'Here I will-be to-live!' And little-mouse began to-live in little-mitten.

paragraphs.target: Прибі́гла жа́бка: «Хто в рукави́чці живе́?» «Я, ми́шка. А ти хто?» «А я жа́бка. Мо́жна й мені́?» І вони́ почали́ жи́ти ра́зом.
paragraphs.source: A little frog came running: 'Who lives in the mitten?' 'I do, the little mouse. And who are you?' 'I'm the little frog. May I come in too?' And they began to live together.
paragraphs.source_literal: Ran-up little-frog: 'Who in little-mitten lives?' 'I, little-mouse. And you who?' 'And I little-frog. Possible and to-me?' And they began to-live together.

paragraphs.target: По́тім прибі́г за́йчик, за ним лиси́чка, а за не́ю во́вчик. У рукави́чці ста́ло ма́ло мі́сця, але́ всім було́ те́пло.
paragraphs.source: Then a little hare came running, after him a little fox, and after her a little wolf. There was little room left in the mitten, but everyone was warm.
paragraphs.source_literal: Then ran-up little-hare, after him little-fox, and after her little-wolf. In little-mitten became little of-room, but to-all was warm.

paragraphs.target: Діду́сь помі́тив, що рукави́чки нема́є, і поверну́вся до лі́су. Ми́шка й її́ дру́зі поба́чили його́ й шви́дко побі́гли в ліс.
paragraphs.source: Grandpa noticed that his mitten was gone and went back to the forest. The little mouse and her friends saw him and quickly ran off into the forest.
paragraphs.source_literal: Grandpa noticed, that of-little-mitten there-is-not, and returned to forest. Little-mouse and her friends saw him and quickly ran-off into forest.

paragraphs.target: А діду́сь узя́в свою́ рукави́чку й пішо́в додо́му.
paragraphs.source: And Grandpa took his mitten and went home.
paragraphs.source_literal: And grandpa took own little-mitten and went home.

paragraphs.target: Уве́чері бабу́ся співа́є Марі́йці колиско́ву: «Спи, моє́ со́нечко, спи, моя́ мале́нька. Ко́тик уже́ спить, і ми́шка в рукави́чці спить».
paragraphs.source: In the evening Grandma sings Mariika a lullaby: 'Sleep, my sunshine, sleep, my little one. The kitty is already asleep, and the little mouse is asleep in the mitten.'
paragraphs.source_literal: In-evening grandma sings to-Mariika lullaby: 'Sleep, my little-sun, sleep, my little. Kitty already sleeps, and little-mouse in little-mitten sleeps.'

paragraphs.target: «Хай спля́ть твої́ о́чка до ра́нку. У на́шій хати́нці ти́хо й те́пло».
paragraphs.source: 'Let your little eyes sleep till morning. It is quiet and warm in our little house.'
paragraphs.source_literal: 'Let sleep your little-eyes till morning. In our little-house quiet and warm.'

questions.prompt: 'Рукави́чка' comes from 'рукави́ця', mitten, just as 'лиси́чка' comes from 'лиси́ця', fox. What happens to 'ц' before the suffix '-к-'?
questions.explanation: Before a diminutive suffix 'ц' becomes 'ч', as in 'со́нце', 'со́нечко'. The 'ц' before '-і' in 'у руці́' is a different change.

choices: 'little eyes', from 'о́ко', with 'к' becoming 'ч' before the suffix
questions.explanation: 'О́чко' is the diminutive of 'о́ко', and 'о́чка' is its plural. The 'к' becomes 'ч' before the suffix '-к-', as in 'я́блучко'.

paragraphs.target: Ще сто ро́ків тому́ в украї́нській мо́ві були́ слова́ для жіно́к, які́ працю́ють: вчи́телька, лі́карка, продавчи́ня. Такі́ іме́нники назива́ють фемініти́вами.
paragraphs.source: A hundred years ago Ukrainian already had words for working women: 'вчи́телька', 'лі́карка', 'продавчи́ня'. Such nouns are called feminitives.
paragraphs.source_literal: Still hundred years ago in Ukrainian language were words for women, who work: teacher-woman, doctor-woman, shop-assistant-woman. Such nouns they-call by-feminitives.

paragraphs.target: У двадця́тому столі́тті в докуме́нтах про жіно́к ча́сто писа́ли в чолові́чому ро́ді: дире́ктор, інжене́р, а́втор. Фемініти́ви тоді́ вважа́ли слова́ми для розмо́ви, а не для докуме́нтів.
paragraphs.source: In the twentieth century, documents often referred to women in the masculine: 'дире́ктор', 'інжене́р', 'а́втор'. Feminitives were then considered words for conversation, not for documents.
paragraphs.source_literal: In twentieth century in documents about women often they-wrote in masculine gender: director, engineer, author. Feminitives then they-considered by-words for conversation, and not for documents.

paragraphs.target: У правопи́сі дві ти́сячі дев’ятна́дцятого ро́ку напи́сано, як утво́рювати фемініти́ви. Найчасті́ше до чолові́чого сло́ва додаю́ть той са́мий су́фікс, що й у сло́ві «студе́нтка»: а́вторка, дире́кторка, інжене́рка.
paragraphs.source: The orthography of 2019 sets out how feminitives are formed. Most often the same suffix as in 'студе́нтка' is added to the masculine word: 'а́вторка', 'дире́кторка', 'інжене́рка'.
paragraphs.source_literal: In orthography two thousand of-nineteenth of-year written, how to-form feminitives. Most-often to masculine word they-add that same suffix, as also in word 'student-woman': author-woman, director-woman, engineer-woman.

paragraphs.target: І́нші фемініти́ви ма́ють і́нші су́фікси: керівни́к і керівни́ця, письме́нник і письме́нниця, хіру́рг і хіру́ргиня.
paragraphs.source: Other feminitives have other suffixes: 'керівни́к' and 'керівни́ця', 'письме́нник' and 'письме́нниця', 'хіру́рг' and 'хіру́ргиня'.
paragraphs.source_literal: Other feminitives have other suffixes: head and head-woman, writer and writer-woman, surgeon and surgeon-woman.

paragraphs.target: Сього́дні фемініти́ви мо́жна поба́чити в нови́нах, в університе́тах і в оголо́шеннях про робо́ту. Мовозна́вці ка́жуть, що вони́ важли́ві для украї́нської, бо в ній ко́жен іме́нник ма́є рід.
paragraphs.source: Today feminitives can be seen in the news, at universities and in job advertisements. Linguists say that they are important for Ukrainian, because every noun in it has a gender.
paragraphs.source_literal: Today feminitives possible to-see in news, in universities and in announcements about work. Language-knowers say, that they important for Ukrainian, because in it every noun has gender.

paragraphs.target: Не всім ці слова́ подо́баються, тому́ про жі́нку ще ча́сто ка́жуть «лі́кар». Але́ до нови́х слів лю́ди шви́дко звика́ють.
paragraphs.source: Not everyone likes these words, so people still often say 'лі́кар' about a woman. But people quickly get used to new words.
paragraphs.source_literal: Not to-all these words please, therefore about woman still often they-say 'doctor'. But to new words people quickly get-used.

questions.prompt: According to the article, how did documents of the twentieth century often name a woman's profession?
choices: With the masculine noun, such as 'дире́ктор'
With the feminine noun, such as 'дире́кторка'
questions.explanation: 'В докуме́нтах про жіно́к ча́сто писа́ли в чолові́чому ро́ді', in the masculine gender, and feminitives were thought of as words for conversation.

questions.prompt: Which pair is formed in the same way as 'керівни́к' and 'керівни́ця'?
questions.explanation: In both pairs '-иця' takes the place of '-ик'. 'А́вторка' adds '-ка', and 'хіру́ргиня' adds '-иня'.

questions.prompt: Why, according to linguists, are feminitives important for Ukrainian?
choices: Because they are shorter than the masculine nouns
Because every Ukrainian noun has a grammatical gender
questions.explanation: 'Бо в ній ко́жен іме́нник ма́є рід': in a language in which every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, a woman is readily named by a feminine noun.

questions.prompt: What does the article say about new words?
choices: People quickly get used to them
They are used only in documents
questions.explanation: 'До нови́х слів лю́ди шви́дко звика́ють': people quickly get used to new words.

exercises.prompt: Match the diminutives with their meanings
What does a diminutive suffix add to a noun?
choices: The meaning 'small', 'dear to the speaker', or both
exercises.explanation: 'Ко́тик' is a small cat or a cat the speaker is fond of. The gender stays that of 'кіт', masculine.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the diminutive of 'ха́та'?
exercises.explanation: 'Хати́нка' adds the suffixes '-ин-' and '-к-' to 'ха́та'. 'Ха́ти' and 'ха́тою' are forms of 'ха́та' itself, the genitive and the instrumental.

exercises.prompt: A diminutive keeps the gender of the word it comes from. What gender is 'со́нечко'?
exercises.explanation: 'Со́нце' is neuter, so 'со́нечко' is neuter too: 'моє́ со́нечко'.

choices: Grandma is singing the little girl a lullaby.
Grandma is singing the little boy a lullaby.
Grandma is reading the little girl a story.

exercises.hint_source: A little boy and a little girl are out for a walk.
Mariika gives Grandma her little hand.
exercises.explanation: Both diminutives of 'рука́' fit: 'руче́ньку' is the more tender. The 'к' of 'рука́' becomes 'ч' before the suffix, and the accusative ends in '-у'.

exercises.prompt_target: У на́шого сусі́да ___ хати́нка бі́ля рі́чки.
exercises.hint_source: Our neighbor has a little cottage by the river.
exercises.explanation: 'Мале́нький', built with '-еньк-', agrees with the feminine 'хати́нка'; the plain 'мала́' is also correct.

exercises.prompt: 'Ні́жка' comes from 'нога́'. Which changes does it show?
choices: 'г' becomes 'ж', and 'о' becomes 'і' in the closed syllable 'ніж'
exercises.explanation: Before the suffix '-к-', 'г' becomes 'ж'. The 'ж' closes the first syllable, and in a closed syllable 'о' becomes 'і'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the diminutive of 'кіт' spelled 'ко́тик', with 'о'?
choices: The suffix '-ик' opens the syllable, so 'і' returns to 'о', as in 'кота́'
exercises.explanation: 'Кіт' is one closed syllable, so it has 'і'. In 'ко-тик' the syllable is open, and 'о' returns.

exercises.prompt: At a post office counter a customer says: 'Да́йте, будь ла́ска, ру́чку.' What does he want?
exercises.explanation: 'Ру́чка', once a diminutive of 'рука́', is now the everyday word for a pen and a handle.

exercises.prompt: Taras shows a photo of a friend's huge new house and says: 'Гарне́нька хати́нка!' What does he mean?
choices: The house is small and pretty
The house belongs to a child
He is joking: the house is anything but a cottage
exercises.explanation: Said of something large, a diminutive is ironic and means the opposite of what it says.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings

exercises.explanation: 'Телефо́н' is masculine, so the possessive adjective has its short masculine form 'ма́мин'.
'Кни́га' is feminine. The ending '-а' opens the syllable, so the 'і' of 'та́тів' becomes 'о': 'та́това'.

exercises.prompt: Complete 'Це ... вікно́' to say 'This is Dad's window'.
exercises.explanation: 'Вікно́' is neuter, so the neuter form 'та́тове' is needed. 'Та́тів' is masculine, 'та́това' feminine and 'та́тові' plural.

choices: Olena's sister works as a programmer.
Olena's brother works as a doctor.
Olena's brother works as a programmer.

exercises.hint_source: Mom's cup is on the table.

exercises.prompt: Which suffix makes the feminine of 'керівни́к'?
exercises.explanation: Nouns in '-ник' and '-ик' replace '-ик' with '-иця': 'керівни́ця', 'письме́нниця'.

exercises.hint_source: She is the head of our hospital.
exercises.explanation: For a woman the feminine 'керівни́ця' is used; 'на́шої лі́карні' is the genitive, 'of our hospital'.

exercises.prompt_target: Вона́ ___ і пи́ше кни́ги для діте́й.
exercises.hint_source: She is a writer and writes books for children.
exercises.explanation: 'Письме́нник' forms its feminine with '-иця' in place of '-ик'.

exercises.hint_source: She works as a surgeon in a large hospital.
exercises.explanation: For a woman, 'хіру́рг' takes '-иня': 'хіру́ргиня'. After 'працюва́ти' the profession is in the instrumental, so the ending is '-ею', as in 'продавчи́нею'.

choices: On 'ка', because the suffix is stressed
On 'а', because a feminine in '-ка' usually keeps the stress of the masculine noun
exercises.explanation: 'А́втор', 'а́вторка', as 'лі́кар', 'лі́карка' and 'студе́нт', 'студе́нтка'.

choices: Andrii's coffee is the best in the city.
Andrii's tea is the best in the city.
Andrii's coffee is the most expensive in the city.

exercises.prompt_source: She is the author of this book.

exercises.prompt: Complete 'Це ... кни́га' to say 'This is Andrii's book'.
exercises.explanation: 'Кни́га' is feminine. The ending opens the syllable, and 'ї' after a vowel returns to 'є': 'Андрі́єва'.
A prefix stands before the root. Here 'на-', on, joins the root 'пис' of 'писа́ти': something written on a surface.
'Пис' carries the meaning 'write'. 'Під-' is a prefix, and 'письм-' is the root with the suffix '-ьм-'.

exercises.prompt: Which word does not belong to the family of 'друг'?
exercises.explanation: 'Дру́жба', 'по́друга' and 'дружи́на' share the root of 'друг', which becomes 'друж' before the suffixes of 'дру́жба' and 'дружи́на'. 'Дя́дько', uncle, has another root.
'Бабу́син' from 'бабу́ся', in the locative feminine to agree with 'кварти́рі': the hard-adjective ending '-ій'.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana is out for a walk with her mom's friend.
exercises.explanation: After 'з' meaning 'with', 'по́другою' is instrumental, and 'ма́мин' agrees with it: 'ма́миною'.
'Дзвони́ти' takes the dative, 'дру́гові', and the possessive agrees: 'та́товому', with 'о' because the ending opens the syllable.

exercises.prompt_source: My aunt's daughter lives in Lviv.

exercises.explanation: The possessive adjective 'Окса́нина' agrees with the feminine 'кни́га'; the genitive 'кни́га Окса́ни' is also correct.

exercises.prompt_source: Whose kitten is this? It's Sofia's.
answers: Чий це ко́тик? Це Со́фіїн ко́тик.
Чий це ко́тик? Це ко́тик Со́фії.
exercises.explanation: 'Чий' agrees with the masculine 'ко́тик'. After a vowel the suffix is '-їн': 'Со́фія', 'Со́фіїн'.

exercises.prompt_source: She is a manager, and he is a writer.
exercises.explanation: Each person gets the form of the profession that matches them: 'керівни́ця' for her, 'письме́нник' for him.
'Дру́жба' is feminine, so 'на́ша' and 'важли́ва' are feminine too.
